title: Choosing a rabbit breed for meat
subtitle: Growth rate, carcase yield, and temperament in the main UK meat breeds.
excerpt: Meat rabbit breeds are selected for fast growth, efficient feed conversion, and a high ratio of loin and leg meat to total live weight. New Zealand White is the commercial benchmark. Several traditional breeds suit small holdings where calm handling and outdoor conditions matter alongside production. Here is a comparison of the main UK options.
sourceNotes: British Rabbit Council, breed standards and meat breed information. Rare Breeds Survival Trust, rabbit breed profiles. RWAF, rabbit care factsheets.

glossaryTerms.definition: A meat rabbit slaughtered between 8 and 12 weeks of age, when dressed weight reaches 1.2–1.8 kg. Named for the US style of preparation; in UK contexts the same animal is often called a 'young rabbit' or simply a 'table rabbit'.

at 8 to 12 weeks, or as a 'roaster' at 12 to 16 weeks for a larger carcase. Breed selection affects how quickly this weight is reached and how the animal handles small-scale outdoor conditions.

The standard against which all meat breeds are measured. Reaches 2 kg live weight by 8 weeks on a pellet-only diet. White fur and pink eyes; calm temperament. Less suited to outdoor housing than heritage breeds because it was developed for intensive cage production. Does raise litters of 8 to 10 kits reliably.

White with dark nose, ears, feet, and tail. Slightly slower growing than the New Zealand White (2 kg at 9 to 10 weeks) but with slightly better meat-to-bone ratio. Common in commercial cross-breeding programmes, often with the New Zealand White as the terminal sire.

A very large breed (5 to 7 kg adult weight) sometimes chosen for larger table weights, but growth rate is slow compared to commercial breeds and feed conversion is poor. Better suited to producing a single large roaster than efficient fryer production.
Silver: a heritage silver-grey breed with a long carcase and good loin. Calm temperament; suits outdoor housing. Slower growing than commercial breeds but produces excellent flavour.
Chinchilla: developed in the UK, good meat conformation. Attractive grey coat that can be tanned or sold.
What to prioritise for a small holding

For a small outdoor system, a heritage breed or a commercial-heritage cross works better than a pure New Zealand White. Heritage breeds suit outdoor handling and grass-based conditions; commercial breeds were developed for intensive cage systems. The slower growth rate is not a disadvantage for home use. Pick a breed with a calm doe and good mothering instincts.
